new.title: Look down on Napoleon's tomb
new.desc: Under the gold-leafed Dôme des Invalides, Napoleon lies in a massive red quartzite sarcophagus on a green granite base, finished twenty years after his remains came home from Saint Helena. The setting is as theatrical as the man.
new.tip: The same ticket covers the Musée de l'Armée; do not skip the Plans-Reliefs in the attic, a collection of huge scale models of fortified towns started for Louis XIV.

new.title: Find The Thinker in the Musée Rodin garden
new.desc: Rodin left his work to France on condition that the Hôtel Biron became his museum. The Thinker and the unfinished Gates of Hell stand outdoors among the roses, which makes this one of the calmest museum visits in Paris.
new.tip: Start in the garden while your legs are fresh, then go inside the mansion; there is a casual café under the trees behind the house.

new.title: See the Impressionists in a railway station
new.desc: The Musée d'Orsay fills the Gare d'Orsay, a station built for the 1900 World's Fair, and holds the largest Impressionist and post-Impressionist collection anywhere: Monet, Manet, Renoir, Degas, Van Gogh. The great station clock still hangs over the main hall.
new.tip: Book a timed ticket online and head straight for the top floor galleries, then work your way down to the sculpture nave.

new.title: Watch Foucault's pendulum swing in the Panthéon
new.desc: In 1851 Léon Foucault hung a 67 metre pendulum under this dome to prove that the Earth turns, and a copy still swings there today. Down in the crypt rest Voltaire, Victor Hugo, Marie Curie and Josephine Baker.
new.tip: Stand still for a few minutes and watch the pendulum drift along its scale; in the warmer months you can also climb up to the colonnade around the dome.

new.title: Sit on the steps of the Arènes de Lutèce
new.desc: A Roman arena from the 1st century hides behind an ordinary row of apartment buildings. It was dug up when rue Monge was built and saved from becoming a tram depot by a committee led by Victor Hugo.
new.tip: Slip in through the passage at 47 rue Monge with a sandwich; it is a neighbourhood park now, so expect a kickabout on the old arena floor.

new.title: Follow the brass line in Saint-Sulpice
new.desc: A thin brass meridian runs across the floor of this huge church to a marble obelisk. It is an 18th-century astronomical instrument: sunlight from a hole high in the south window crosses the line at true noon and climbs the obelisk in midwinter.
new.tip: Come around solar noon on a clear day to see the disc of light on the floor, and ignore what The Da Vinci Code says about it: this is not the Paris Meridian.

new.title: Find the Fontaine Médicis
new.desc: Tucked into a shady corner of the Jardin du Luxembourg, this 17th-century grotto fountain ends in a long, dark basin. The jealous giant Polyphemus looms over the lovers Acis and Galatea, added when the fountain was moved here in the 1860s.
new.tip: Enter by the gate near the Odéon theatre and turn left; grab one of the green metal chairs and stay a while.
new.q: Fontaine Médicis, Jardin du Luxembourg, Paris

new.title: Walk among the animals at Deyrolle
new.desc: Since 1831 this shop has dealt in taxidermy, insects and natural history. Upstairs is a cabinet of curiosities with lions, zebras and drawers full of butterflies, rebuilt after a fire destroyed much of it in 2008.
new.tip: The ground floor looks like a garden shop; take the staircase at the back. It is a shop, not a museum, so look with your eyes and keep the camera down.

new.title: Walk the giant murals of boulevard Vincent Auriol
new.desc: The 13th has turned its tower blocks into an open-air gallery. Between Chevaleret and Place d'Italie you pass Shepard Fairey's Marianne, D*Face's 25 metre Turncoat, an Invader mosaic on the Pitié-Salpêtrière hospital and a dozen more.
new.tip: Walk it uphill from Chevaleret, then ride metro line 6 back: it runs on a viaduct here, so you see the murals at eye level from the train.

new.title: Wander the Cité florale
new.desc: Six tiny cobbled streets named after flowers, lined with small houses and overflowing gardens, built in 1928 on a meadow that the Bièvre river used to flood. The ground was too soft for apartment blocks, which is why this village survives.
new.tip: Go in from rue Brillat-Savarin near Place de Rungis in late spring, when the wisteria on rue des Glycines is out. People live here, so keep your voice down.
new.q: Cité florale, rue des Glycines, Paris

new.title: Peek through the gate of La Ruche
new.desc: This round artists' colony was put together in 1902 from leftovers of the 1900 World's Fair, including a wine pavilion with an iron frame by Gustave Eiffel. Chagall, Modigliani, Soutine and Léger all worked here, and around fifty artists still do.
new.tip: You only get a glimpse through the ivy-covered gate on passage de Dantzig unless the small exhibition room is open; pair it with the cottage lane Villa Santos-Dumont nearby.
new.q: La Ruche, 2 passage de Dantzig, Paris

new.title: Step into Bourdelle's studio
new.desc: Sculptor Antoine Bourdelle worked in this studio behind Montparnasse station from 1885 until 1929, and it still smells of wood and plaster. Giant bronzes fill the courtyards, and the museum reopened in 2023 after a two year renovation.
new.tip: The permanent collection is free to visit; it is closed on Mondays.

new.title: Meet the Lady and the Unicorn at Cluny
new.desc: The national museum of the Middle Ages keeps six 15th-century tapestries of a lady, a lion and a unicorn: five for the senses and a sixth nobody quite agrees on. The building itself swallows a Roman bathhouse with its cold room still vaulted.
new.tip: Look for the Pillar of the Boatmen in the Roman frigidarium, a carved stone from the 1st century and one of the oldest things in Paris.

new.title: Visit the Statue of Liberty on the Île aux Cygnes
new.desc: A quarter-scale Liberty, a bit over 11 metres tall, has stood at the tip of this narrow artificial island since 1889. She was turned around in 1937 and now looks west, towards her big sister in New York.
new.tip: Walk the whole tree-lined Allée des Cygnes from Pont de Bir-Hakeim: 850 metres with the Seine on both sides and the Eiffel Tower behind you.
new.q: Statue de la Liberté, Île aux Cygnes, Paris

new.title: Eat a galette on rue du Montparnasse
new.desc: Bretons arriving at Montparnasse station did not walk far before settling, so this short street is still lined with crêperies. Crêperie de Josselin draws the longest queue for its double-layered buckwheat galette, the Couple.
new.tip: Drink cider with it, brut rather than sweet. If the Josselin queue is too long, Chez Jeanne and Le Petit Josselin across the street won a local taste test.
new.q: Crêperie de Josselin, 67 rue du Montparnasse, Paris

new.title: Drink mint tea at the Grande Mosquée
new.desc: The 1926 mosque, with its 33 metre minaret and tiled Moorish courtyards, has a tea room where waiters carry trays of sweet mint tea between fig trees and sparrows. Honey-soaked pastries are chosen from the counter inside.
new.tip: The tea room has its own entrance on the corner facing the Jardin des Plantes; the mosque gardens can be visited separately on any day but Friday.
new.q: Grande Mosquée de Paris salon de thé, rue Geoffroy-Saint-Hilaire, Paris

new.title: Buy a slice of miche at Poilâne
new.desc: Pierre Poilâne opened this bakery on rue du Cherche-Midi in 1932, and the family still bakes its round two kilo sourdough loaf in a wood-fired oven. The little butter biscuits are called punitions, punishments.
new.tip: You do not have to take a whole loaf: ask for a quarter or a few slices, and take a bag of punitions for the walk.

new.title: Order a chocolat chaud at Café de Flore
new.desc: Open since the 1880s on the corner of boulevard Saint-Germain, the Flore was the living room of Picasso, Queneau and the post-war existentialists, and it still awards its own literary prize every year. Its rival Les Deux Magots is one door down.
new.tip: It is pricey, so treat it as theatre: take one drink upstairs, where regulars sit and it is quieter than the terrace.

new.title: Graze your way down rue Mouffetard
new.desc: One of the oldest streets in Paris, a Roman road that runs downhill from Place de la Contrescarpe to the church of Saint-Médard. The lower end is a daily street market of cheesemongers, fruit stalls, bakers and a wine shop that pours tastings on the pavement.
new.tip: Go in the morning and start at the top so you walk downhill; many stalls shut on Mondays.
new.q: Rue Mouffetard market, Square Saint-Médard, Paris

new.title: Slurp a pho on avenue de Choisy
new.desc: The Triangle de Choisy is the heart of Paris's biggest Asian quarter, and a steaming bowl of Vietnamese beef noodle soup is its signature lunch. Pho 14 is the name that keeps coming up for good value and fast service.
new.tip: There is usually a short queue outside at lunchtime and it moves fast. For dessert, try the green tea cakes at pastry shop Bán Tân Tân on the same avenue.

new.title: Have dinner on the Butte-aux-Cailles
new.desc: This hilltop of low houses and cobbles only joined Paris in 1860 and still feels like a village. Le Temps des Cerises is its classic no-frills French bistro, named after the song of the Paris Commune, whose fighters held this hill in 1871.
new.tip: They do not take reservations, so arrive early; Chez Gladines around the corner serves enormous Basque salads if it is full.
new.q: Le Temps des Cerises, 18 rue de la Butte-aux-Cailles, Paris

new.title: Eat under the dome at La Coupole
new.desc: This vast Art Deco brasserie opened in December 1927 and became the canteen of Montparnasse: Cocteau, Giacometti, Josephine Baker and Man Ray were early regulars. It still serves until late at night.
new.tip: Seafood platters are the house speciality; ask for a table in the middle of the room, under the dome, rather than by the windows.
new.q: La Coupole, 102 boulevard du Montparnasse, Paris

new.title: Pack a picnic on rue Cler
new.desc: A pedestrian street of food shops a few minutes from the Eiffel Tower: fromagers, charcutiers, bakers, a fishmonger, wine. This is where the 7th arrondissement does its daily shopping.
new.tip: Come Tuesday to Saturday when everything is open, fill a bag and carry it five minutes to the lawns of the Champ de Mars.

new.title: Share a pizza at La Felicità
new.desc: A giant Italian food market inside Station F, the old freight hall turned start-up campus: a pizzeria, a trattoria, a beer garden and a cocktail bar under one roof, with DJ sets and concerts at the weekend.
new.tip: You order at each counter and carry your own tray; come early on Friday or Saturday evening, when half of the 13th turns up.
new.q: La Felicità, 5 parvis Alan Turing, Paris

new.title: Climb the Eiffel Tower on foot
new.desc: Skip the lift and take the stairs: a little over 300 steps to the first floor and as many again to the second, inside the iron lattice with Paris opening up between the girders. From there a lift goes on to the top.
new.tip: The stairs queue is usually the shortest. After dark the tower sparkles for five minutes on the hour, best watched from the Champ de Mars.

new.title: Go down into the Catacombs
new.desc: The bones of more than six million Parisians, moved out of overflowing cemeteries, are stacked in neat walls along old quarry tunnels deep under Place Denfert-Rochereau. It is eerie, cold and oddly beautiful.
new.tip: Book a timed ticket online in advance, because walk-up places are rare. Bring a jumper, and note that the exit is a few streets away from the entrance.

new.title: Get lost in Shakespeare and Company
new.desc: George Whitman opened this English-language bookshop facing Notre-Dame in 1951 and let travelling writers sleep among the shelves in exchange for a few hours' work. More than 30,000 of these Tumbleweeds have stayed since.
new.tip: Climb to the reading library upstairs, where you may sit and read for as long as you like, then have your book stamped at the till.
new.q: Shakespeare and Company, 37 rue de la Bûcherie, Paris

new.title: Sail a toy boat in the Jardin du Luxembourg
new.desc: Children have pushed wooden sailing boats across the octagonal Grand Bassin in front of the Senate for generations. Around it are the puppet theatre, an orchard of old apple and pear varieties and Bartholdi's small model of the Statue of Liberty.
new.tip: The boat hire stand works on fine afternoons, mostly Wednesdays, weekends and school holidays; you get a stick to push your boat off the edge.
new.q: Grand Bassin, Jardin du Luxembourg, Paris

new.title: Swim in spring water at the Butte-aux-Cailles pool
new.desc: This 1924 red-brick pool with its vaulted concrete hall is fed by an artesian well, drilled almost 600 metres down, whose water comes up warm. There are two outdoor pools as well as the indoor one.
new.tip: Bring a swimming cap, which is compulsory in Paris pools. Locals fill their bottles for free at the well fountain on Place Paul-Verlaine outside.
new.q: Piscine de la Butte-aux-Cailles, 5 place Paul-Verlaine, Paris

new.title: Walk the old railway of the Petite Ceinture
new.desc: The disused ring railway around Paris has become a 1.3 kilometre nature walk through the 15th, between Place Balard and rue Olivier-de-Serres. The rails are still there, and wild plants have been left to take over the embankments.
new.tip: Use the stairs of the former Vaugirard-Ceinture station on rue de Vaugirard, or the lift at rue Olivier-de-Serres, and finish in Parc Georges-Brassens.
new.q: Petite Ceinture du 15e, rue Olivier-de-Serres, Paris

new.title: Browse the weekend book market at Parc Georges-Brassens
new.desc: Every weekend since 1987, dealers in old and second-hand books set up under the iron horse hall of the former Vaugirard slaughterhouses. The park behind it has a small vineyard, beehives and two bronze bulls guarding the gate.
new.tip: Enter at 104 rue Brancion on Saturday or Sunday; prices are friendlier than on the Seine quays and browsing costs nothing.
new.q: Marché du livre ancien et d'occasion, 104 rue Brancion, Paris

new.title: Hunt for treasure at the Puces de Vanves
new.desc: Around 400 dealers line two avenues every weekend morning at the only antiques and flea market inside the Paris city limits, running since 1905. It is smaller and far friendlier than Saint-Ouen: old postcards, silver, enamel signs, linen.
new.tip: Be there early on Saturday or Sunday, because stalls start packing up around lunchtime. Metro Porte de Vanves, and bring cash.
new.q: Marché aux puces de la Porte de Vanves, avenue Marc-Sangnier, Paris

new.title: Dance to live jazz at the Caveau de la Huchette
new.desc: A vaulted stone cellar in the Latin Quarter that has been a jazz club since the late 1940s, with a band on stage and couples swinging on the floor. Its sign and its piano turn up in the film La La Land.
new.tip: The band starts mid-evening and nobody minds if you cannot dance; go on a weeknight for more room on the floor.
new.q: Caveau de la Huchette, 5 rue de la Huchette, Paris

new.title: Fill a basket at Tang Frères
new.desc: The mother ship of Paris's Asian supermarkets, opened on avenue d'Ivry in 1981 by two brothers from Laos. Aisles of fresh herbs, dim sum, sauces, exotic fruit and rice cookers pull in shoppers from across the city.
new.tip: Afterwards look for the Buddhist temple hidden in the car park beneath the Olympiades towers, a few doors along avenue d'Ivry.

new.title: Spread a blanket in Parc Montsouris
new.desc: A hilly English-style park from the 1870s at the southern edge of the city, with a lake, an island full of birds and an abandoned stretch of the Petite Ceinture railway cutting through it. A stone marker from 1806 recalls the Paris Meridian.
new.tip: Take RER B to Cité Universitaire, which stops inside the park, and cross the road afterwards to stroll among the national houses of the student campus.
